evidence: Cic. de Or. 1.249: peregrīnī atque advenae (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: One who has come (advenīre) to a place and lives there, as against indigena, a native. Used of birds as well: cranes and storks are advenae (Plin. NH 10.61).

terms.gloss: incomer; someone living in a place not his own
evidence: Sall. Cat. 31.7: inquilīnus cīvis urbis Rōmae (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Its everyday sense is a tenant or lodger (see tenant). Sallust’s Catiline sneers at Cicero, born in Arpinum, as a citizen who only lodges in Rome; so of a newcomer to a country it is contemptuous.

terms.gloss: move in, go to live (in a place)
evidence: Cic. Phil. 13.34: in domum et in paternōs hortōs immigrābit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Classically to move into a house or a place, with in and the accusative; to move to a new country it is the same verb, with the country as the place. The simple migrāre is to move house, to emigrate.

phrases.latin: Advena est; ē Graeciā hūc migrāvit.
phrases.english: He’s not from here: he moved here from Greece.
